subject: chemistry
title: Rate of reaction
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Rate of reaction — AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification, section 4.6.1.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry (AQA) practice covering Rate of reaction, specification section 4.6.1.
final_note: You worked through Rate of reaction — 28 specification statements.

concepts.def: How quickly a reaction proceeds. It can be found by measuring the quantity of a reactant used or the quantity of product formed over time.
The average rate over a period of time: mean rate of reaction = (quantity of reactant used) / (time taken), or (quantity of product formed) / (time taken).
How much of a starting substance has been consumed in a given time, measured as a mass in grams or as a volume in cm³ (moles at Higher Tier).
How much of a new substance has been made in a given time, measured as a mass in grams or as a volume in cm³ (moles at Higher Tier).
The units of rate of reaction may be given as g/s or cm³ /s, because a quantity is divided by a time.
At Higher Tier the quantity of reactants may be given in moles, and the rate of reaction is then given in mol/s.
A graph of the quantity of product formed, or of reactant used up, plotted against time. Its steepness at any point shows how fast the reaction is going.
A straight line drawn so that it just touches a curve at one point. Its slope is used as a measure of the rate of reaction at that moment.
The change in the y quantity divided by the change in time along the tangent, calculated as a measure of rate of reaction at a specific time.
The concentrations of reactants in solution, the pressure of reacting gases, the surface area of solid reactants, the temperature and the presence of catalysts.
The amount of a dissolved substance in a given volume of solution. A more concentrated solution has more reactant particles in the same volume.
How tightly gas particles are packed. Raising the pressure of reacting gases puts more particles into the same volume.
The area of solid exposed to the other reactant. Breaking a solid into smaller pieces exposes more of it.
The cloudiness of a mixture. A reaction that makes an insoluble solid grows cloudy, and the time for a mark to disappear can be timed.
A testable prediction about how one variable will affect another, which the investigation is then designed to test.
Chemical reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy.
How many collisions happen each second. Increasing it increases the rate of reaction.
The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react.
The surface area of a solid divided by its volume. Smaller pieces of the same mass have a larger surface area to volume ratio.
A simple idea used with collision theory: doubling the number of particles in a given volume roughly doubles the collision frequency, and so roughly doubles the rate.
A substance that changes the rate of a chemical reaction but is not used up during the reaction. Different reactions need different catalysts.
A biological catalyst. Enzymes act as catalysts in biological systems.
The route a reaction takes from reactants to products. A catalyst provides a different pathway that has a lower activation energy.
An energy diagram for a reaction. For a catalysed reaction it is drawn with a lower hump, while the reactants and products stay at the same energies.

mcqs.q: A student follows the reaction between marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid, which gives off carbon dioxide. Which set of measurements would allow the mean rate of reaction to be worked out?
options: The volume of gas collected, together with the time taken to collect it
The total volume of gas given off at the end, and nothing else
The time taken until the fizzing finally stops, and nothing more
The temperature of the mixture, measured every ten seconds
mcqs.explain: The rate of a chemical reaction can be found by measuring the quantity of product formed over time, so a quantity and a time are both needed.

mcqs.q: In a reaction, 3.6 g of magnesium ribbon is used up in 180 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?
options: 0.020 g/min
50 g/s
mcqs.explain: mean rate of reaction = (quantity of reactant used) / (time taken) = 3.6 g / 180 s.

mcqs.q: A gas syringe collects 12 cm³ of gas in 8 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?
options: 0.67 cm³ /s
1.5 cm³ /min
1.5 cm³ /s
96 cm³ /s
mcqs.explain: mean rate of reaction = (quantity of product formed) / (time taken) = 12 cm³ / 8 s.

mcqs.q: The specification states how the quantity of a reactant or product may be measured. Which pair does it give?
options: The concentration in mol/dm³ or the temperature in °C
The mass in grams or the total time taken in seconds
The volume in cm³ or the pressure of the gas in pascals
The mass measured in grams or the volume in cm³
mcqs.explain: The quantity of reactant or product can be measured by the mass in grams or by a volume in cm³ .

mcqs.q: Which of these is given in the specification as a unit of rate of reaction?
options: s/cm³
cm³ /s
mol/dm³
cm³
mcqs.explain: The units of rate of reaction may be given as g/s or cm³ /s.

mcqs.q: (HT) In a Higher Tier question the quantity of a reactant is given in moles. In which unit should the rate of reaction then be given?
options: mol/dm³
s /mol
mol
mol/s
mcqs.explain: For the Higher Tier, units for rate of reaction may be given in mol/s.

mcqs.q: (HT) In a reaction, 0.60 mol of hydrogen is produced in 30 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?
options: 0.020 mol/min
0.020 mol/s
18 mol/s
mcqs.explain: 0.60 mol divided by 30 s, with the rate given in mol/s as the Higher Tier requires.

mcqs.q: A flask of reacting mixture stands on a balance. The mass falls from 82.50 g to 81.90 g in 120 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?
mcqs.explain: The mass lost is 0.60 g, and 0.60 g divided by 120 s gives 0.0050 g/s.

mcqs.q: Experiment X produces 30 cm³ of gas in 20 s. Experiment Y produces 45 cm³ of gas in 45 s. Which statement about the mean rates is correct?
options: Y is faster, because Y produces the larger total volume of gas
Y is faster, because the reaction in Y was allowed to run for longer
The mean rates are equal, since both experiments make gas steadily
X is faster: its mean rate is 1.5 cm³ /s and the mean rate of Y is 1.0 cm³ /s
mcqs.explain: Each quantity is divided by its own time before the two are compared.

mcqs.q: A graph of the volume of gas produced against time is steep at first and then becomes less steep. What does this shape show?
options: The volume of gas begins to fall once the curve bends over
The reaction speeds up steadily as more product forms
The reaction runs at one steady rate the whole way
The reaction is fastest at the start, and then slows down
mcqs.explain: Steepness of the curve is a measure of rate, so a falling steepness means a falling rate.

mcqs.q: The line on a graph of volume of gas against time becomes horizontal after 80 s. What does this tell you?
options: No more gas is being made, so the reaction has ended
Gas is now being made at a steady, constant rate
The reaction is still speeding up, but more gradually
The gas is now being used up again in a reverse reaction
mcqs.explain: A horizontal line has zero gradient, so the rate is zero and the reaction has stopped.

mcqs.q: A student needs the rate of reaction at 30 s from a curved graph of volume of gas against time. What should the student do?
options: Draw a tangent at 30 s and work out its slope
Read the volume off the curve at 30 s and use that
Join the origin to the point at 30 s and use that slope
Divide the final volume by the total time of the run
mcqs.explain: The specification requires a tangent to be drawn and its slope used as a measure of the rate.

mcqs.q: (HT) A tangent drawn to a volume-time curve at 20 s passes through the points (10 s, 12 cm³ ) and (30 s, 52 cm³ ). What is the rate of reaction at 20 s?
options: 2.0 cm³ /s
0.50 cm³ /s
40 cm³ /s
2.0 cm³
mcqs.explain: The gradient is (52 - 12) cm³ divided by (30 - 10) s = 40 / 20 = 2.0 cm³ /s.

mcqs.q: Which list contains only factors that the specification says affect the rate of a chemical reaction?
options: Concentration, pressure of gases, surface area, temperature, time
Concentration, pressure of gases, surface area, temperature, catalysts
Concentration, colour of the reactants, temperature, stirring, catalysts
Concentration, pressure of gases, surface area, pH, volume of flask
mcqs.explain: This is exactly the list the specification gives.

mcqs.q: A reaction mixture is cooled from 40 °C to 20 °C. What happens to the rate of the reaction?
options: It increases, because cooling packs the particles closer together
It decreases, as collisions are less frequent and less energetic
It is unchanged, since temperature affects only the final amount made
It decreases, but only if a catalyst is taken out as well
mcqs.explain: Students should be able to recall that lowering the temperature lowers the rate.

mcqs.q: Required practical 5 investigates how changes in concentration affect the rate of reaction. Which pair of methods does the specification require?
options: Measuring the volume of a gas, and following the temperature rise in the flask
Measuring the volume of a gas, and following a colour change or turbidity
Measuring the temperature rise, and following a colour change or turbidity
Weighing the solid left behind, and following the volume of the solution used
mcqs.explain: These are the two methods named in Required practical 5.

mcqs.q: Required practical 5 should involve developing a hypothesis. Which of these is a suitable hypothesis for the investigation?
options: The higher the concentration of the acid, the faster gas will be produced
Measure the volume of gas every ten seconds for each concentration used
Add the acid to the magnesium and time each reaction with a stopwatch
Concentration and rate of reaction are connected in some way
mcqs.explain: It is a testable prediction linking the independent variable to the dependent variable.

mcqs.q: According to collision theory, when can a reaction between two particles take place?
options: Whenever they collide, no matter how gently they hit each other
Only when the collision itself gives out enough energy
Only when they collide with at least the activation energy
Whenever they are in the same container as each other
mcqs.explain: Reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy.

mcqs.q: What is meant by the activation energy of a reaction?
options: The energy given out as the products are formed
The energy that is given out when the particles collide and react
The minimum energy that particles must have in order to react
The total energy needed to make all the particles react
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's definition of activation energy.

mcqs.q: Why does increasing the concentration of hydrochloric acid increase the rate of its reaction with magnesium?
options: The acid particles move faster, so their collisions carry more energy
The activation energy of the reaction is lowered by the extra acid
More particles in the same volume means more frequent collisions
Each single collision becomes much more likely to end in a reaction
mcqs.explain: Increasing the concentration of reactants in solution increases the frequency of collisions.

mcqs.q: A 5 g strip of magnesium and 5 g of magnesium powder are added to separate beakers of the same acid. Why does the powder react faster?
options: There is simply more magnesium in the powder than in the strip
It has a larger surface area to volume ratio, so collisions are more frequent
The powder particles move faster, so the collisions are more energetic
The powder must lower the activation energy needed by the reaction
mcqs.explain: The effect of the size of the pieces is explained in terms of surface area to volume ratio.

mcqs.q: Why does raising the temperature increase the rate of a reaction? Give the full reason.
options: Collisions are more frequent, and that is the whole of the reason why
Collisions happen more often, and nothing else about them changes
The activation energy of the reaction falls as it is heated
Collisions are more frequent and more of them are energetic enough
mcqs.explain: Increasing the temperature increases the frequency of collisions and makes the collisions more energetic.

mcqs.q: Two gases react together. Why does increasing the pressure of the gases increase the rate of reaction?
options: Squeezing the particles closer together makes each collision harder
Raising the pressure lowers the energy that a successful collision needs
There are more gas particles present than there were before
The particles are in a smaller volume, so they collide more often
mcqs.explain: Increasing the pressure of reacting gases increases the frequency of collisions.

mcqs.q: Doubling the concentration of a solution roughly doubles the rate of reaction. Using simple ideas about proportionality, what should halving the concentration do?
options: Cut the rate to a quarter, since the rate depends on the square
Cut the rate by more than half, as the particles also move slower
Leave the rate unchanged, since the same amount of acid still reacts
Roughly halve the rate, as collisions become half as frequent
mcqs.explain: Simple proportionality: half the particles in the same volume gives about half the collision frequency.

mcqs.q: Which statement about catalysts is correct?
options: A catalyst is used up slowly, so more must be added as it goes
One catalyst will speed up any reaction that it is added to
A catalyst changes the rate of a reaction but is not used up by it
A catalyst makes a reaction produce more of the product
mcqs.explain: Catalysts change the rate of chemical reactions but are not used up during the reaction.

mcqs.q: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a chemical reaction?
options: It provides a different pathway with a lower activation energy
It lowers the activation energy of the original reaction pathway
It speeds up any reaction at all, as catalysts always do
It makes the reaction produce more product, so it goes faster
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's explanation of catalytic action.

mcqs.q: On a reaction profile for a catalysed reaction, how does the catalysed curve differ from the uncatalysed one?
options: Its hump is lower, and the reactants and products are unchanged
Its hump is lower, and the products end up at a lower energy too
Its hump is lower, and it makes more product as well
The hump is the same, but the curve reaches products sooner
mcqs.explain: The lower hump shows the lower activation energy of the new pathway; the energy levels stay the same.

mcqs.q: The equation for a reaction is 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. A solid is added to the flask, the reaction speeds up, and the solid is recovered unchanged at the end. What is the solid?
options: A reactant, because it was added to the flask before the reaction started
A catalyst, as it speeds the reaction up and is not in the equation
A product, because it was there in the flask at the end of the reaction
An enzyme, because it is a solid substance that speeds the reaction up
mcqs.explain: Catalysts are identified from their effect on the rate and from their absence from the chemical equation.

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.6.1 Rate of reaction
